title: Cost & latency optimisation
summary: Cut the cost and response time of your LLM app by choosing the right model, caching context, and streaming output.
objectives: Understand how token pricing turns inputs and outputs into money
Measure cost with token counting before you send a request
Pick the right model for each task to balance cost and quality
Use prompt caching to slash the cost of repeated context
Reduce latency with streaming and smaller, focused prompts
Use the Batches API for non-urgent, high-volume jobs
Build the habit of measuring before optimising

quiz.q: In the Claude API, you pay separately for input tokens and output tokens. Which is usually more expensive per token?
quiz.why: Output tokens cost more per token than input tokens (e.g. Sonnet 4.6 is $3 input vs $15 output per million), so keeping responses short saves the most money.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of prompt caching when you reuse a large document across many requests?
options: Cached tokens are served at roughly 10% of the normal input price
It removes the need for an API key
quiz.why: Cache reads cost about a tenth of the normal input price, so reusing a cached prefix can cut input costs by up to ninety percent.

quiz.q: Which technique most directly improves the *perceived* latency of a chat app — the time before the user sees anything?
options: Streaming the response token by token
quiz.why: Streaming shows tokens as they are generated, so the user sees output almost immediately instead of waiting for the full response.

quiz.q: Why should you count tokens with the API before sending a large request, rather than estimating with a generic tokenizer?
quiz.answer: Token counts are model-specific; generic tokenizers like tiktoken undercount Claude tokens, so using messages.count_tokens gives an accurate cost estimate.
quiz.why: The count_tokens endpoint uses Claude's own tokenizer, so your cost estimate matches what you will actually be billed.

quiz.q: You have 50,000 product reviews to classify overnight, and the results are not needed immediately. Which approach is most cost-effective?
quiz.answer: Use the Batches API, which processes requests asynchronously at 50% of the standard price.
quiz.why: Batch processing trades immediacy for a 50% discount, ideal for large, non-latency-sensitive jobs.

quiz.q: True or false — the fastest way to cut cost is always to switch to the cheapest model.
quiz.why: False. A cheap model that gives wrong answers may need retries or human fixes; match the model to the task and measure before deciding.

body_markdown:
## Why cost and latency matter

Once your app works, two numbers decide whether it survives in production: how much each request **costs** and how long users **wait**. A demo that calls the most expensive model on every keystroke is fine for a weekend project, but it will burn your budget and frustrate users at scale.

The good news: a handful of techniques can cut both dramatically — often by an order of magnitude — without rewriting your logic.

## How token pricing works

The API bills per **token** (roughly three-quarters of a word). You pay separately for the **input** (your prompt) and the **output** (the model's reply), and output is several times more expensive per token. For example, Claude Sonnet 4.6 is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens.

So the two biggest levers are: send less input, and ask for shorter output.

## Measure before you optimise

Never guess at cost — count. The `count_tokens` endpoint uses Claude's own tokenizer, so the number matches your bill. Do not use generic tokenizers like tiktoken; they undercount Claude tokens.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
resp = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": open("report.md").read()}],
)
print(resp.input_tokens)
# Estimated input cost = input_tokens * 3 / 1_000_000  (dollars)
```

## Choose the right model

Not every task needs your smartest model. Use a tiered approach: a small, fast model for simple work and a larger one only where quality really matters.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

# Cheap and fast — good for simple classification
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-4-5",
    max_tokens=10,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Classify as positive or negative: Loved it!"}],
)
print(resp.content[0].text)
```

Keep your key in an environment variable (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`); never hard-code it.

## Cache repeated context

If many requests share a big chunk of text — a long document, a system prompt, few-shot examples — cache it. The first request writes the cache; later requests read it at roughly a tenth of the input price.

```python
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[{
        "type": "text",
        "text": large_document_text,
        "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
    }],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise the key points"}],
)
print(resp.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)  # tokens served cheaply from cache
```

Caching is a **prefix match**: keep stable content first and volatile content (timestamps, IDs) last, or you will silently invalidate the cache.

## Reduce latency

Latency is about how fast users *feel* your app, not just total compute. Two habits help most:

- **Stream** the response so users see text immediately instead of waiting for the whole reply.
- **Trim** the prompt — shorter input and a sensible `max_tokens` both speed things up.

For large, non-urgent jobs (overnight classification, bulk summaries), use the **Batches API**: it runs asynchronously at 50% of the standard price.

## Your task

Take one feature of your app, run `count_tokens` on a real request, then try one optimisation — a smaller model, caching, or streaming — and compare the before and after.

slides.title: Caching is a prefix match
bullets: Any change to the prefix invalidates the cache.
Keep stable content first.
Put timestamps and IDs last.
slides.narration: One important rule: caching is a prefix match. Any byte change anywhere in the cached prefix invalidates everything after it. So keep your stable content — the frozen system prompt, the document — at the front, and push volatile things like timestamps and request I Ds to the very end. Get this wrong and the cache silently never hits.

slides.title: Reduce latency
bullets: Stream so users see text immediately.
Trim the prompt and set a sensible max_tokens.
Latency is about how fast it feels.
slides.code:
with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=msgs,
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="")
slides.narration: Latency is about how fast your app feels, not just total compute. The biggest win is streaming: show tokens as they're generated, so the user sees output almost instantly instead of waiting for the whole reply. Beyond that, trim your prompt and set a sensible max tokens — shorter input and output both make every response quicker.

slides.narration: For large jobs where the results aren't needed this second — classifying fifty thousand reviews overnight, summarising a backlog — use the Batches A P I. It processes requests asynchronously and charges fifty percent of the standard price. You trade immediacy for a half-price discount, which is a great deal when nobody is waiting on the answer.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Optimising before measuring.
Always grabbing the cheapest model.
Breaking the cache with a timestamp up front.
Leaving max_tokens far too high.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps. One: optimising before measuring — always count first. Two: always grabbing the cheapest model; a wrong answer that needs a retry or a human fix can cost more than doing it right. Three: breaking the cache by putting a timestamp at the start of the prompt. And four: leaving max tokens set far higher than you need, which slows responses and risks runaway cost.
